title: Calculus of Vector-Valued Functions
lead: The derivative of a vector-valued function $\kvecr(t)$ is the limit of a difference quotient, found by differentiating its component functions; it is a tangent vector to the curve, and dividing it by its length gives the principal unit tangent vector $\kvecT(t).$ The derivative rules carry over, with three product rules, and vector-valued functions are integrated component by component.
objectives: Write an expression for the derivative of a vector-valued function.
Find the tangent vector at a point for a given position vector.
Find the unit tangent vector at a point for a given position vector and explain its significance.
Calculate the definite integral of a vector-valued function.
summary_html:
• To calculate the derivative of a vector-valued function, calculate the derivatives of the component functions, then put them back into a new vector-valued function.
  • Many of the properties of differentiation from the Introduction to Derivatives also apply to vector-valued functions.
  • The derivative of a vector-valued function $\kvecr(t)$ is also a tangent vector to the curve. The unit tangent vector $\kvecT(t)$ is calculated by dividing the derivative of a vector-valued function by its magnitude.
  • The antiderivative of a vector-valued function is found by finding the antiderivatives of the component functions, then putting them back together in a vector-valued function.
  • The definite integral of a vector-valued function is found by finding the definite integrals of the component functions, then putting them back together in a vector-valued function.

exercises.prompt:
A particle moves on a circular path of radius b according to the function $\textbf{r}(t)=b\;\cos (\omega t)\;\textbf{i}+b\;\sin (\omega t)\;\textbf{j},$ where $\omega$ is the angular velocity, $d\theta /dt.$

Find the velocity function and show that $\textbf{v}(t)$ is always orthogonal to $\textbf{r}(t).$

answer.solution: $\textbf{r}'(t)=-b\omega \;\sin (\omega t)\;\textbf{i}+b\omega \;\cos (\omega t)\;\textbf{j}.$ To show orthogonality, note that $\textbf{r}'(t)\cdot \;\textbf{r}(t)=0.$

exercises.prompt:
A particle moves on a circular path of radius b according to the function $\textbf{r}(t)=b\;\cos (\omega t)\;\textbf{i}+b\;\sin (\omega t)\;\textbf{j},$ where $\omega$ is the angular velocity, $d\theta /dt.$

Show that the speed of the particle is proportional to the angular velocity.

answer.solution: With $\mathbf{r}(t)=b\cos(\omega t)\,\mathbf{i}+b\sin(\omega t)\,\mathbf{j},$ the velocity is $\mathbf{v}(t)=\mathbf{r}\'(t)=-b\omega\sin(\omega t)\,\mathbf{i}+b\omega\cos(\omega t)\,\mathbf{j},$ so the speed is $\|\mathbf{v}(t)\|=\sqrt{b^{2}\omega^{2}\sin^{2}(\omega t)+b^{2}\omega^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega t)}=\sqrt{b^{2}\omega^{2}}=b\omega$ for $\omega\gt 0.$ The speed is the constant $b$ times the angular velocity $\omega$: proportional to it, with the radius as the constant of proportionality.

exercises.prompt: Evaluate $\frac{d}{dt}[\;\textbf{u}(t)\;\times \;\mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)]$ given $\textbf{u}(t)=t^{2}\;\textbf{i}-2t\;\textbf{j}+\;\textbf{k}.$
Evaluate $\int_0^{3}\| t\;\textbf{i}+t^{2}\;\textbf{j}\| dt.$
Show that if the speed of a particle traveling along a curve represented by a vector-valued function is constant, then the velocity function is always perpendicular to the acceleration function.

answer.solution: $\begin{array}{rll}\| \;\textbf{v}(t)\| & = & k \\ \textbf{v}(t)\cdot \;\textbf{v}(t) & = & k \\ \frac{d}{dt}(\;\textbf{v}(t)\cdot \;\textbf{v}(t)) & = & \frac{d}{dt}k=0 \\ \textbf{v}(t)\cdot \;\textbf{v}'(t)+\;\textbf{v}'(t)\cdot \;\textbf{v}(t) & = & 0 \\ 2\;\textbf{v}(t)\cdot \;\textbf{v}'(t) & = & 0 \\ \textbf{v}(t)\cdot \;\textbf{v}'(t) & = & 0.\end{array}$<sup class="fn" data-note="c-e73"></sup> The last statement implies that the velocity and acceleration are perpendicular or orthogonal.

exercises.prompt:
Given $\textbf{r}(t)=t\;\textbf{i}+2\;\sin t\;\textbf{j}+2\;\cos t\;\textbf{k}$ and $\textbf{u}(t)=\frac{1}{t}\;\textbf{i}+2\;\sin t\;\textbf{j}+2\;\cos t\;\textbf{k},$ find the following:

Now, use the product rule for the derivative of the cross product of two vectors and show this result is the same as the answer for the preceding problem.

answer.solution: With $\mathbf{r}\'(t)=\mathbf{i}+2\cos t\,\mathbf{j}-2\sin t\,\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{u}\'(t)=-\frac{1}{t^{2}}\,\mathbf{i}+2\cos t\,\mathbf{j}-2\sin t\,\mathbf{k},$ the product rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{r}\'\times\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{u}\'.$ Here $\mathbf{r}\'\times\mathbf{u}=\langle 4,\,-\frac{2\sin t}{t}-2\cos t,\,2\sin t-\frac{2\cos t}{t}\rangle$ and $\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{u}\'=\langle -4,\,2t\sin t-\frac{2\cos t}{t^{2}},\,2t\cos t+\frac{2\sin t}{t^{2}}\rangle.$ Their sum is $\langle 0,\,2\sin t\,(t-\frac{1}{t})-2\cos t\,(1+\frac{1}{t^{2}}),\,2\sin t\,(1+\frac{1}{t^{2}})+2\cos t\,(t-\frac{1}{t})\rangle,$ the derivative of $\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{u}=\langle 0,\,2\cos t\,(\frac{1}{t}-t),\,2\sin t\,(t-\frac{1}{t})\rangle$ found directly.

footnotes.html: The key’s second line reads $\mathbf{v}(t)\cdot\mathbf{v}(t)=k$; from $\|\mathbf{v}(t)\|=k$ it is $\mathbf{v}(t)\cdot\mathbf{v}(t)=k^{2},$ still a constant, so the rest of the argument stands.
The key writes the last component as $0\;\mathbf{j}$; the third component of the acceleration is along $\mathbf{k}$: $\mathbf{a}(t)=-\cos t\;\mathbf{i}-\sin t\;\mathbf{j}+0\;\mathbf{k}.$

The key ends with $2\cos t\,(t-\frac{2}{t})$; differentiating $2\sin t\,(t-\frac{1}{t})$ gives $2\cos t\,(t-\frac{1}{t})+2\sin t\,(1+\frac{1}{t^{2}}),$ so the last component is $2\sin t\,(1+\frac{1}{t^{2}})+2\cos t\,(t-\frac{1}{t}).$

Three terms of the key are misprinted. The $\mathbf{j}$-components of $\frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{u}'(t)\times\mathbf{u}(t)]$ and $\frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{u}(t)\times\mathbf{u}'(t)]$ are $72t^{5}+24$ and $-72t^{5}-24,$ not $24+75t^{2}$ and $-24-75t^{2},$ and $\frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{u}(t)\cdot\mathbf{u}'(t)]=720t^{8}-960t^{3}+6t^{2}+4.$
